title: Association of Organic Cation Transporter 1 With Intolerance to Metformin in Type 2 Diabetes: A GoDARTS Study
authors: Dujic T, Zhou K, Donnelly LA, Tavendale R, Palmer CNA, Pearson ER
followUp: prescribing records of incident metformin users from 1 January 1994 to 1 June 2011
population: Patients with type 2 diabetes in Tayside, Scotland, from the Genetics of Diabetes Audit and Research Tayside Study: 251 classified as intolerant, defined as stopping immediate-release metformin within 6 months and switching to another oral agent, and 1915 as tolerant, defined as taking 2000 mg or more daily for more than 6 months; patients with serum creatinine above 120 micromol/L were excluded
funder: The Wellcome Trust United Kingdom Type 2 Diabetes Case Control Collection (GoDARTS) cohort collection was funded by the Wellcome Trust and informatics support is provided by the Chief Scientist Office, Scotland. This work was specifically supported by a European Foundation for the Study of Diabetes Albert Renold Travel Fellowship; the senior author holds a Wellcome Trust New Investigator Award (102820/Z/13/Z).
authorConflicts: We declare no conflict of interest.
result: Women and older people were more likely to be intolerant of metformin. Concomitant use of medicines known to inhibit OCT1 transport was associated with intolerance (odds ratio 1.63, 95% CI 1.22 to 2.17, p = 0.001), as was carriage of two reduced-function OCT1 alleles against one or none (2.41, 1.48 to 3.93, p < 0.001); individuals with two reduced-function alleles who also took OCT1 inhibitors were over four times more likely to be intolerant (4.13, 2.09 to 8.16, p < 0.001). Five reduced-function variants were studied: R61C, C88R, G401S, M420del and G465R. Drugs shown in vitro to inhibit OCT1 include tricyclic antidepressants, proton pump inhibitors, alpha-adrenoceptor antagonists and the calcium-channel blockers verapamil and diltiazem. The paper states as background, citing earlier literature, that gastrointestinal side effects occur in 20% to 30% of patients taking metformin and that about 5% develop severe symptoms and discontinue the drug, and that the intolerance phenotype used here is a proxy derived from prescribing patterns.
